Transgender comic Jordan Gray hit overnight stardom at the Edinburgh Fringe in 2022. Her new show at the Adelaide Cabaret Festival deals with the aftermath.

“It changed my life by a factor of a hundred,” says Jordan Gray. In 2022, she premiered her astonishing show Is It a Bird? at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe. It corralled her powers as a joke writer, singer, keyboard player and all-round force of nature to narrate her experiences since coming out as a trans woman at 25. The titular pun posed the question: why do people revere Batman, who identifies as a bat, but so often baulk at trans people living their true identity?

In the first days of the festival, Gray received a boxful of flyers her producers had printed for her to hand out on the street to punters. The five-star reviews and full houses were already flowing and she never even opened the box. Career-defining highlights kept coming: Sir Ian McKellen attended one night and Gray coaxed him onstage to “knight” her. At another show, her grandfather hobbled onstage with his walking stick to hold her hand above his head in triumph.

Still, some elements of the show proved divisive when she took it to a wider audience on Channel 4’s Friday Night Live special. “It was well-received and we won a BAFTA for it, but there was a small but very vocal contingent that did not think it was very funny,” Gray says. “The culmination of [Is It a Bird?] is that I end up naked onstage, which is easy and fun to do after you’ve ingratiated yourself with the audience for 45 minutes. But when I [got naked] on live TV in the UK after one minute, that culminated in a lot of angry rhetoric and some death threats. That’s not uncommon for anybody in this industry, but when you’re transgender, there is a specific flavour to it.”

Gray didn’t respond to the threats but says they are hard to shake. They were front of mind on a recent visit to Los Angeles to take part in Netflix’s filming of the live Stamptown variety show. “I had guns on the brain all the time,” she says. “I thought that someone was going to shoot me, though it was absolutely lovely and I had nothing to worry about. The only way to deal with it, really, is by killing with kindness. I just wish those people would come to the show and see how funny and lighthearted it is.”

Gray tackles this dramatic chapter of her career head-on in her new show, Is That a Cock in Your Pocket, or Are You Just Here To Kill Me?, a “dead split between stand-up and musical comedy” that she is performing at the Adelaide Cabaret Festival this month. “I thought it’d be funny to write a song about it. We don’t really have guns in the UK, but a lot of the threats had a gun adjacent to them, so I thought I’d give the next show a bit of a gunslinger vibe, like an old Hollywood thing. I just loved the idea of taking ownership of it.”

Beyond tackling the death threats, Gray says her new show is a “direct response” to her sudden fame. “It did change my life completely overnight – there is no following something like that. But I think it’s quite funny to lean into the difficult second album syndrome of it all, so I open with a song about that.”

As with many apparent overnight success stories, Gray had worked on her stagecraft and writing skills for many years. She was a creative kid, though her parents differed on the value they placed on artistic pursuits. “When you’ve got one parent that’s overly praising you and one that’s very withholding, it’s like an internal combustion engine. My dad didn’t treat being a comedian as a real job – not until I was making more money than him! Then it was suddenly legit and he’s very supportive now. But from the get-go, my mum was really supportive. I run on that – positive reinforcement is how you get me to do stuff. If I feel like I’ve disappointed somebody, I’ll curl up in a ball and die. I need to be continuously impressive.”

“Even if you’re up there blowing balloons out of your arse – which I will not be doing but which is a great skill to have – cabaret’s still an inherently political act.”

As a teenager, she sang (or screamed) in a death metal band. While many metal musicians are reluctant to switch even to a different microgenre, Gray ditched metal altogether for pop when her bandmates moved away, initially making music on a toy keyboard with a computer microphone duct-taped on, using a pair of stockings stretched over a coathanger as a homemade pop shield. Restlessly moving across genres and moods, she performed and recorded under the moniker Tall Dark Friend and became a working musician, if not a household name.

While Gray seems a natural and exuberant performer, she relishes periods of relative isolation, including working as a writer. She has published two novels and a nonfiction book, Beautiful Lights: Living with Hallucinations, about her experiences with hallucinogen persisting perception disorder. She recently signed a deal to write her memoir and is looking forward to another stretch of stillness.

In 2014, she moved with her then fiancée to Sweden, expecting a bucolic break from life as a musician. “I spent a lot of time looking after horses,” she recalls. “There’s something nice about being out in nature that reminds you of how small we are.”

One day as she was chopping wood in a field, some strangers walked past and she had a feeling they were seeing someone who wasn’t really her. It was an epiphany that would change everything. “I realised something was quite wrong. I had started trying to get really bulky, doing Insanity Workout, this 18-DVD box set of exercises. But I was overcompensating. I came back to England, realised what was going on, and quite quickly transitioned.”

As if to make up for lost time, she threw herself back into music. A couple of years later, she had some success on The Voice UK, where she was the first transgender contestant – and reached the semi-finals. She found her eclectic output counted against her. “I don’t want to be pigeonholed, but you realise it’s quite important to be pigeonholed if you’re pursuing a music career. Otherwise, how on earth do people know what you make?”

A moment of happenstance on that show pointed the way to a future career. The costume designers had created a red suit for Gray that was almost the exact same colour as a couch she was sitting on during an interview. Sensing the opportunity for a visual gag, she lay down as if to disappear into the furniture. The laughs were immediate and addictive.

Digging into the work of singular American comedian Maria Bamford was also pivotal, unlocking exciting possibilities for raw and revealing autobiographical comedy. “I learnt more about her past and her struggles with intrusive thoughts,” says Gray. “I’ve always been a very repressed person, so to hear her talking about that was really cool. Somebody that’s gone through so much and come out the other side making hilarious stuff? That gave me hope that I could do that, because, just like most people, my mental health record is not completely spotless.”

Gray’s first comedy gig was a roaring success, or at least she thinks it was. “It was the day after I had a boob job, and I was in a dressing-gown with loads of surgical wrapping. I remember it being great, but I was really high on painkillers, so I don’t know! I was thinking I was going to show up in a dressing-gown everywhere and that would be my bit. You very quickly learn that comedy is more than just wearing a dressing-gown and having a silly haircut.”

Her years as a musician were instrumental in her comedy, and not only because she included songs in her work. “I think what happens with comedians when they start is that they’re like, ‘I have to earn being here’, where I was like, ‘Well, I’ve been up here for 10 years, it’s just that I’ve been singing instead of telling jokes.’ ”

Early in her comedy career, Gray became aware that she was subconsciously standing on one foot during routines. She realised it was a tic to stop her going on autopilot and not being present in the room, a common pitfall for comedians, who inevitably tell the same jokes hundreds of times. This revelation was the unlikely origin of her physically expressive style as a comic, a penchant for using every inch of the stage.

“Now I consciously contort myself into whatever strange shapes I can, so that I’m still in the room,” Gray says. “It’s like if I keep going at 11 out of 10, it shows the audience how much I care. You’ve got people like Marc Maron – who I think is really funny – who sit on a stool the whole time to rapturous applause. I just happen to have chosen the path where you keep going and going and going until you can’t breathe. The idiot in this scenario really is probably me.”

While Gray’s work defiantly centres her identity as a trans woman, prominent comedic voices such as Ricky Gervais and Dave Chappelle have had huge success with anti-trans rhetoric. “It’s a shame because I held both those men in very high regard,” Gray says. “The Office was defining for a lot of people. [Gervais] brought ironic bigotry back into TV – you’re laughing at how much of a blind spot that character has to bigotry. I think it shows a lack of self-awareness from two men that I thought had a huge degree of self-awareness. I think they gave up learning, and it’s not a good colour on them, but good luck to them. If they can turn it around in the coming years, that would be great to see.”

With Is It a Bird?, Gray crafted a show that was generous and inclusive. Some of her proudest moments have been parents telling her they understand their transgender children better after watching it. Yet she doesn’t consider herself an authority on transgender issues. “Even I don’t know all the terms. I have excited transgender people coming up to me now and asking me about being poly and I can’t even riff on that. I don’t know about it and I have to learn.”

Reflecting that she “enjoys being pulled in a lot of different directions”, Gray wrote and starred in a sitcom, Transaction, and has dreams of being a showrunner à la Tina Fey, potentially doing something superhero-themed. There are more music projects in the works as well, though she prefers the social element of comedy over music. She was heartened to discover that comics regularly mingle with peers and punters alike after gigs. “In music, we take ourselves way too seriously to maintain an air of mystique,” she says, with a laugh. “Musicians at the low level that I was at are like squids. You never really meet, you just cross over in the dark.”

Is It a Bird?’s blend of physicality, theatrical music and nudity also opened doors in the world of cabaret. Gray often appeared as the only comedian on a mixed bill, performing a song or a section of the show alongside clowns, circus acts and genre-crossing oddballs.

“I never felt like I deserved the title ‘cabaret artist’, but to me, it represents stand-up with a greater degree of freedom,” she says. “It’s higher risk, higher reward. It was born out of a very, very difficult time in Weimar-era Germany, so even if you’re up there blowing balloons out of your arse – which I will not be doing but which is a great skill to have – it’s still an inherently political act. You feel like you’re attached to a lineage of something very powerful when you’re doing cabaret.”

Daniel Herborn is a journalist and novelist.
